image.caption: In Blender, you can insert background images so that you can easily trace around the shape

content: One way to import an image to Blender is to have your File Explorer window open in front of the Blender window, and then [k]Click+Drag[/k] the file into your scene.

image.caption: Dragging an image into Blender

content: This will result in the creation of an [b]Empty[/b], which you will see in the Outliner.

image.caption: An Empty created after inserting an image

content: The "empty" is a single coordinate point with no additional geometry. Because an empty has no volume and surface, it cannot be rendered. Still it can be used as a handle for many purposes.
Displays as six lines, initially with one pointing in each of the +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, and -Z axis directions.
Displays as arrows, initially pointing in the positive X, Y, and Z axis directions, each with a label.
Displays as a single arrow, initially pointing in the +Z axis direction.
Displays as a circle initially in the XZ plane.
Displays as a cube, initially aligned to the XYZ axes.
Displays as an implied sphere defined by three circles. Initially, the circles are aligned, one each, to the X, Y, and Z axes.
Displays as a cone, initially pointing in the +Y axis direction.
Empties can display images. This can be used to create reference images, including blueprints or character sheets to model from. The image is displayed regardless of the 3D display mode.
Empty Displays settings can be accessed from [kbd]Properties > Object Data > Empty[/kbd] panel.
Offset the image origin (where 1.0 represents the width/height of the image).

table.td: Always display on top of other objects.
Always display behind of other objects.
Display both the front and back of the empty.
Only display the front of the image.
Only display the back of the image.

content: Show in orthographic view.
Show in perspective view.
Only displays the image contents when the view is aligned with the object’s local axis.
Blends the image with the background. The value slider adjusts the opacity of the image, changing how much of the image is blended with the background.

image.caption: Empty Display Types.

content: Depending on how your view was positioned, your image may have come in rotated or off-center. You can fix this by pressing [k]Alt-R[/k] for the rotation, and [k]Alt-G[/k] to return the image to the 3D cursor.

image.caption: An imported image's rotation and position may need to be adjusted before work can begin
After removing Rotation and Position modifications

content: With the image in place, [k]1[/k] to go into Front View and then [k]R,X,90[/k] to stand it up straight. Then [k[G,Z[/k] to move it into position above the floor. You might find it hard to see the grid behind the image, so go to the image properties on the right, and change the Opacity to somewhere between 0.2 and 0.25. If you need to [k]G,X[/k] to line it up along the x-axis as well.

image.caption: Standing the image up in Front View
Moving the image above the floor
Changing the image's Opacity property

content: Now, your dinosaur may be 2.5m tall, but we want it to be around 3m, we need to scale it up. First, [k]Shift-S[/k] to move the 3D cursor to the World Origin if needed. Then, change the Transform Pivot Point to 3D Cursor. Now when you [k]S[/k] scale the image to 3m tall, it will scale around the 3D cursor, keeping its feet on the floor. Last, [k]G,Y[/k] and move it back about 2 units, so that you can model in front of it.

image.caption: Moving the 3D cursor to World Origin
Changing the Transform Pivot Point to 3D cursor
Scaling around the 3D cursor
Move the image back so you can model in front of it

content: This time, before inserting the image, [k]Numpad3[/k] to go into Side View so it's positioned correctly. If the image is facing the wrong direction, [k]R,Z,180[/k] will turn it around. Again, bring the Opacity down between 0.2 and 0.25, and position the image above the floor. Scale it up to 3m, and finally, [k]G,X[/k] to move it back 2 units so you can model in front of it.

image.caption: Inserting the image after going into Side View
You can change the direction the image is facing by Rotating around the z-axis
Both reference images in place

content: Finally, rename your images and move them to their own collection. You may also wish to make then un-selectable, so you don't accidentally grab them while working on your model.

image.caption: Organizing your reference images
Image 1 - Tracing around the background images

key_concepts: In order to create the dinosaur body, we are going to start with a Plane and trace out the side image's outline, and then give it depth in order to make the front.

content: In Object Mode, [k]Shift-A,Mesh,Plane[/k] to add a Plane at the 3D cursor. [k]R,Y,90[/k] to stand it upright in front of the side reference image. [k]Ctrl-A,R[/k] to apply the rotation.
[k]Numpad3[/k] to go into Side View, [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode, and [k]1[/k] into Vertex Selection Mode. Also [k]Alt-Z[/k] into X-Ray Mode and if not set, make your Transform Pivot Point the Median.

image.caption: Image 2 - Add a Plane in front of the side reference image
Image 3 - Going into Edit Mode to begin modeling
Image 4 - Setting the Transform Pivot Point to Median

content: We are going to build the dinosaur's body and head first. Begin by positioning the Plane over the hips. Positioning the Plane as seen in Image 5 illustrates how many cuts you will need to match the curve of the body. So [k]Ctrl-R[/k] to do a Loop Cut across the middle, and [k]LMB,LMB[/k] to set that in position. Then drag the middle vertices in place.

Grab the two vertices on the right side of the hips and [k]E[/k] to Extrude them. [k]S[/k] to Scale the right edge down to match the curvature of the outline. Make several extrusions, using [k]G[/k] to Grab and [k]S[/k] to Scale along the way to trace along the reference image's outline.
When you get to the end, there is no need to make the vertices meet at a point, you can leave a square shape at the end of the tail.

Go back to the other end and start Extruding out towards the neck. When you get to the head, you might find that as it curves around the shape you will get shorter edges on one side, that will be fine, since we will adapt the shape as we go along. Don't worry about the mouth, we will be cutting that put later.
This should give you the rough shape; we start of simple and build up the complexity as we go.

image.caption: Image 5 - Tracing the shape of the tail
Image 6 - Tapering off at the end of the tail
Image 7 - Finishing the torso and head

content: There are a few ways you can cut in the mouth; you can wait until after you have extruded the plane out to give depth, or you can cut in while it is still flat. In this case, we are going to cut it in while flat.

[k]Ctrl-R[/k] to add in a Loop Cut across the middle of the shape (Image 8). Normally, you want to be careful about where you add Edge Loops, since this creates more places for topology where you can move around and change the shape. But in this case, we need the topology for the mouth, and we will want more topology later when creating curves for the body.

Zoom in on the head and move the new vertices into place along the upper jaw (Image 9). Then starting from the right-most vertex in the mouth, [k]Ctrl-K[/k] to use the Knife Tool and cut vertices for the lower jaw (Image 10).

image.caption: Image 8 - Adding a Loop Cut across the middle
Image 9 - Tracing the upper jaw
Image 10 - Cutting the lower jaw with the Knife Tool

content: There is a fair bit of detail in the head - a brow ridge (Image 11), eye socket, nostril, and jaw flaps (Image 12). We can use Loop Cuts to add topology for those.
[k]3[/k] to go into Face Selection Mode, select the inner mouth faces, and [k]X,F[/k] to delete them (Image 13).

image.caption: Image 11 - Adding a Loop Cut for the brow ridge
Image 12 - Adding topology for the jaw flap
Image 13 - Deleting the mouth faces

content: Now we want to give the body some volume. We will do this by extruding the shape outwards and mirroring across the x-axis. [k]Numpad1[/k] to go into Front View. Still in Edit Mode, either Box Select all faces or [k]A[/k] to select them all, and move them to middle of the left-side of the body (Image 14). From here we can start pushing the belly out, and extruding the face in later on.
[k]Tab[/k] into Object Mode and add a Mirror Modifier across the x-axis to the Plane (Image 15). If you don't see your mirror at first, try [k]Ctrl-A[/k] and apply all transforms.
[k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode, [k]2[/k] for Edge Selection Mode and select all outer edges (Image 16). Turn on Clipping on the Mirror Modifier and [k]E,X[/k] to join the edges to the mirror.
Last, [k]A,M,B[/k] to get rid of any vertices that are sitting on top of each other.

image.caption: Image 14 - Moving the Plane towards the middle of the left-side
Image 15 - Adding a Mirror Modifier across the x-axis
Image 16 - Selecting the outer edges
Image 17 - Extruding the outline edges together

section.header: Splitting the Screen into Front and Side Views
content: In this part, we will be adding curves to the dinosaur's body, so we will be switching between Front and Side views often. However, instead of frequently switching, it would be easier to see both views on screen. We will also get rid of the Timeline at the bottom of the screen since it's not needed.
Hover the dividing area between the 3D Viewport and the Timeline. The cursor should change to an up/down pointing arrow. [k]RMB[/k] to open the Area Options menu.
[k]RMB[/k] on the border opens the Area Options.
Shows an indicator line that lets you select the area and position where to split. [k]Tab[/k] switches between vertical/horizontal.
Shows the join direction overlay.
Swaps this area with the adjacent one.
With the Area Options open, select [k]Join Areas[/k] and click on the area that you want to remove. Remove the Timeline this way.

image.caption: Image 1 - Opening the Area Options

content: Go to the area divider on the right and open the Area Options. This time, choose [k]Vertical Split[/k]. Split the 3D Viewport so that you have two of them, and set one viewport to Front View and the other to Side View. Make the Front viewport smaller and zoom in on the model. For the Side viewport, rotate the camera so you are viewing the model in perspective. [k]T[/k] will get rid of the Toolbar which will help de-clutter the view, and [k]Alt-Z[/k] will enable/disable the Wireframe. It would be less confusing to enable Wireframe Mode in the Front viewport while disabling it on the Side.

image.caption: Image 2 - Splitting the screen into Front and Side Views

content: Make sure to [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode and [k]3[/k] for Face Selection. We need to taper the dinosaur's mouth, so select the outside faces on the upper jaw that should move in. Zoom in on those faces in both viewports so it's easier to see what you're doing. [k]G,X[/k] and move those faces in slightly. Next, [k]R,Z[/k] to taper the snout in. Make sure you start the rotation in the Perspective viewport so you can be sure the front of the snout is moving inwards. Take a quick look around in the Perspective viewport to make sure it looks okay.

image.caption: Image 3 - Selecting the faces of the upper jaw
Image 4 - Moving the upper jaw faces in
Image 5 - Tapering the dinosaur's snout

content: Now select the faces of the lower jaw. Again, [k]G,X[/k] to move them in, and then [k]R,Z[/k] to taper them inwards. Make sure to move around in the Perspective viewport and adjust as needed until it looks good.

image.caption: Image 6 - Selecting the faces of the lower jaw
Image 7 - Adjusting the lower jaw

content: Grab the faces around the midsection (Image 8) and [k]G,X[/k] to move them out to the widest part of the sketch. If you move around in the Perspective viewport, you see that the shoulders are coming out too drastically (Image 9). [k]2[/k] into Edge mode and select the two edges along the side. [k]G,X[/k] to move them back in (Image 10). Grab the next two edges as well and [k]G,X[/k] move them in.

image.caption: Image 8 - Selecting the dino's mid-section
Image 9 - From a different perspective, the shoulders come out too drastically
Image 10 - Move the top edges inwards to slope the shoulders
Image 11 - Move the next edges inwards

content: Move down to the next two edges in the series and [k]G,X[/k] to move them out. These are the lines for the hips, which should be wider (Image 12). After that, select the next two edges and [k]G,X[/k] and bring them out to make more of a curve as the hips narrow towards the tail (Image 13).

image.caption: Image 12 - Widening the hips
Image 13 - Narrowing towards the tail

content: Now we want to merge the tail into a point. First, turn on [k]Auto Merge Vertices[/k] (Image 14), and then select the back two edges on the tail (Image 15). [k]G,X[/k] and merge them into a point.

image.caption: Image 14 - Auto Merge Vertices
Image 15 - Selecting the tail edges
Image 16 - Tapering the tail into a point

content: Select the two edges closest to the point (Image 17). We want to thin out the tail proportionally, so press [k]O[/k] to turn on Proportional Editing, and then [k]G,X[/k] to thin out the tail (Image 18). Use the [k]WheelUp[/k]/[k]WheelDown[/k] to adjust the regions that get influenced. [k]1[/k] to go into Vertex mode and select the vertices at the tip of the tail. [k]G,G[/k] to edge slide them into a single vertex (Image 19). Take some time to review your shape in the Perspective viewport.

image.caption: Image 17 - Auto Merge Vertices
Image 18 - Thinning out the length of the tail
Image 19 - Tapering the tail into a point

content: The dino shape looks about correct, if somewhat boxy. We want to add some curvature to it now. [k]2[/k] into Edge mode and select the top edge before the one leading into the tail. That edge is part of a triangle face and can't be used for what we're going to do. Go to the edge at the top of the upper jaw and [k]Ctrl-LMB[/k] to select all edges in between (Image 20). We are now going to curve them in; [k]G,G[/k] to Edge Slide them in slightly along the x-axis, and then [k]G,G[/k] to slide them down in the z-axis. This will add a curve to the body (Image 21). Repeat along the bottom edge (Image 22).

image.caption: Image 20 - Selecting the edges for the top curve
Image 21 - Curving the top of the body
Image 22 - Curving the bottom of the body

key_concepts: Review the shape in the Perspective viewport, making adjustments as needed.

content: In the Perspective viewport, [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View and [k]1[/k] for Vertex Mode. If you haven't already [k]Alt-Z[/k] to go into Wireframe Mode. [k].[/k] to zoom in on the dino would also help. Now, we need to decide which face would be best for extruding the legs from. It should be one that is closest to the leg position in the rough sketch (Image 1). Move the faces vertices and any other nearby to adjust to be a little closer to the leg's shape (Image 2). Notice that the face we are choosing is the one that comes out from the side, not directly from the bottom (Image 3). This is because when we extrude, we want to have a gap between the legs.

Lastly, when we extrude the face to make the legs, we will only have four edges to work with, since we're extruding a rectangle. This won't be enough geometry to make a curve, giving our dino blocky legs. If we [k]Ctrl-R[/k] to add a loop cut (Image 4), then we can extrude two faces, giving us six edges that can be used for curving the legs.

image.caption: Image 1 - Selecting the face closest to the leg
Image 2 - Shaping the face to be used for the leg extrusion
Image 3 - Highlight of the face chosen for extrusion
Image 4 - Adding an Edge Loop to create more geometry

content: Select the two faces chosen for the legs and extrude them out to the side (Image 5). [k]G[/k] the two bottom faces and [k]E[/k] those faces out (Image 6).

image.caption: Image 5 - Extruding from the hips
Image 6 - Taking the legs out from the bottom faces

content: Now we need to re-position things. [k]G[/k] to grab the bottom faces and move them more in line with the sketch (Image 7). It's probably too wide at the moment, so [k]S,Shift-X[/k] to scale it but not make the leg thinner (Image 8). In the Front viewport, [k]G[/k] to move it in line with the path of the leg (Image 9). [k]R[/k] to rotate it along the lines of the sketch (Image 10) and then again [k]R[/k] in the Side viewport (Image 11).

image.caption: Image 7 - Re-positioning the bottom faces from the side
Image 8 - Scaling the leg's width
Image 9 - Re-positioning the bottom faces from the front
Image 10 - Rotating from the front
Image 11 - Rotating from the side

content: In the Side viewport, [k]E[/k] the bottom faces again (Image 12) and [k]G[/k] them into position (Image 13). [k]R[/k] to rotate the end of the leg (Image14) and [k]G,X[/k] to move them into position from the front (Image 15). Finally, [k[S[/k] to scale it to the right size (Image 16).

image.caption: Image 12 - Extruding the lower legs
Image 13 - Positioning the lower legs from the side
Image 14 - Rotating the end of the lower leg
Image 15 - Positioning the lower legs from the front
Image 16 - Scaling the ankle

content: [k]E[/k] to extrude the bottom faces again to the top of the foot (Image 17). [k]G[/k] to bring it in from the side and [k]S[/k] to scale it to the right size (Image 18). Again, [k]G[/k], [k]S[/k] to move it into position and scale, this time from the front (Image 19).

image.caption: Image 17 - Extruding to the top of the foot
Image 18 - Adjusting the ankle from the side
Image 19 - Adjusting the ankle from the side

content: [k]E[/k] to extrude down to the bottom of the foot (Image 20). In the Front viewport, [k]S[/k] to scale it to the right width (Image 21). Select the front face and [k]E[/k] to extrude to the end of the foot, before the claws (Image 22). [k]1[/k] to go into Vertex mode and select the top vertices of the face. [k]G,G[/k] to slide them down to make the foot the correct height (Image 23). Select the front face again, and in the Front View, [k]S,X[/k] to scale it to the right width for the claws (Image 24).

image.caption: Image 12 - Extruding the lower legs
Image 13 - Positioning the lower legs from the side
Image 14 - Rotating the end of the lower leg
Image 15 - Positioning the lower legs from the front
Image 16 - Scaling the ankle

content: Turn off Wireless mode [k]Alt-Z[/k] and [k]1[/k] into Vertex mode. Start rounding off the shape. Feel free to add Bevel Cuts across the middle of the thigh in order to round it off.

key_concepts: Review the shape in the Perspective viewport, making adjustments as needed.

content: [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode and select the front face of the foot. [k]NumpadPeriod[/k] to zoom in on it (Image 1). [k]Shift-H[/k] will hide everything but the selected face (Image 2). [k]Ctrl-R[/k] and add 2 loop cuts in the front to make 3 faces (Image 3). These faces will be used to extrude the claws. Afterwrds, [k]Alt-H[/k] to make everything visible again.

image.caption: Image 1 - Zooming in on the front of the foot
Image 2 - Hiding everything but the front of the foot.
Image 3 - Adding Loop Cuts for the claws

content: With the claw faces selected, [k]I,I[/k] to Inset the faces (Image 4), and then [k]E,Y[/k] to extrude them out in the y-axis (Image 5). [k]E,Y[/k] to extrude them out again (Image 6) for the tips of the claws, and [k]S[/k] to scale them down in the Front view(Image 7). Make sure the Transform Pivot Point is set to Individual Origins (Image 8). Last, [k]G[/k], [k]R[/k] to move and rotate the tips of the claws into a better position.

image.caption: Image 4 - Insetting the claw faces
Image 5 - Extruding the claws
Image 6 - Extruding the claws again
Image 7 - Scaling them down in the Front view
Image 8 - Setting the Transform Pivot Point is set to Individual Origins
Image 9 - Positioning the tips of the claws

content: Using the Knife Tool ([k]K[/k]), make cuts from the faces at the front of the foot to the vertices at the top (Image 10) and bottom (Image 11). [k]Alt-Z[/k] into Wireframe Mode and select the faces for the outside claw. [k]R,Z[/k] to rotate it outwards in the z-axis (Image 12) and [k]G,Shift-Z[/k] to move those faces into position (Image 13). Do the same thing for the other claw on the inside (Image 14).

image.caption: Image 10 - Cutting edges at the top of the foot
Image 11 - Cutting edges at the bottom of the foot
Image 12 - Rotating the outside claw
Image 13 - Moving the outside claw back into position
Image 14 - Rotating and moving the inside claw

content: My dinosaur foot has a dramatic instep (Image 15). [k]G[/k] to grab some vertices to move them around until you are satisfied with the shape. Be sure to [k]Numpad7[/k] [k]Numpad9[/k] to get a better view from the bottom as well (Image 16).

image.caption: Image 15 - My dinosaur's instep before adjustments
Image 16 - Reviewing my adjustments from underneath

content: [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode, [k]3[/k] into Face Selection, and [k]Numpad1[/k] into Front View. We need a face we can use to extrude the arms out. We can't use the face directly in the front; when we go to extrude the face the arms will be too close together (Image 1) We want a face more to the side. [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View, and [k]Alt-Z[/k] to make sure the reference image is visible. Select the face closest to the shoulder (Image 2). This face is a little too big, but we can cut it smaller using the Knife Tool ([k]K[/k]) (Image 3).

image.caption: Image 1 - The front face nearest the arms is not a good choice
Image 2 - Choose the face closest to the shoulder
Image 3 - Using the Knife Tool to make the face smaller

content: [k]1[/k] into Vertex Mode and move the vertices around the shoulder closer to the beginning of the arm (Image 4). [k]3[/k] into Face Mode and select that face. Moving into your Front View, [k]E[/k] to extrude the face out (Image 5). Grab the bottom face of the extrusion, and [k]E[/k] to extrude it out to the elbow (Image 6), and then [k]S[/k] to scale it down so it's roughly in line (Image 7). Again with the bottom face selected, [k]E[/k] to extrude, [k]G[/k] to move it onto place, and [k]S[/k] to scale it in around the wrist (Image 8). Last, [k]E[/k], [k]S[/k] to end the arm at the wrist (Image 9).

image.caption: Image 4 - Moving the vertices into position around the shoulder
Image 5 - Extruding the shoulder out
Image 6 - Extruding the arm to the elbow
Image 7 -Scaling the face in line with the reference image
Image 8 - Taking the arm out to the wrist
Image 9 - Ending the arm with the claws

content: [k]Alt-Z[/k] to turn off X-Ray Mode and review the changes. The top of the should looks rather boxy (Image 10); we want to smooth that out. [k]2[/k] into Edge Mode, select the top outside edge and [k]G,G[/k] to slide it down the outside of the shoulder, then [k]G,G[/k] to slide it back towards the body (Image 11). The arms now have a nice low poly feel to them and don't really need to be rounded any more. If you want to, you can [k]S[/k] to scale in that top edge, but it isn't absolutely needed.

image.caption: Image 10 - A boxy shoulder
Image 11 - Rounding it out

content: In Side View, we can see that the edges around the neck aren't spaced evenly (Image 12). [k]Alt-LMB[/k] to select the edges and [k]G,G[/k] to create more even separation between them (Image 13). We do this because right now if viewed from the side or the top, the dino has a rather fat neck. We can fix this by shrinking the middle part of the neck slightly. [k]3[/k] into Face Mode, and [k]Alt-LMB[/k] to select the face loop around the middle (Image 14). [k]S[/k] to scale that in slightly, but not too much. Since we have a Mirror Modifier applied, we can [k]G,X[/k] and bring it in towards the center, as long as clipping is on this will clip the sides together (Image 15).

image.caption: Image 12 - The neck edges
Image 13 - Evening out the separation between edge loops
Image 14 - Selecting the middle face loop
Image 15 - Shrinking the neck

content: [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View and [k]Alt-Z[/k] to turn on X-Ray Mode. A great way for quickly creating more topology in an area is to select the faces around that area and [k]I[/k] to inset so suddenly you've got a lot more vertices to play with (Image 16). Then [k]1[/k] into Vertex Mode and [k]G[/k] to move the vertices around into an eye shape (Image 17). In the other viewport move around to see how the eye looks from the side. Things probably will look out of place (Image 18), so [k]G,X[/k] to move the vertices around until we have a general eye shape (Image 19). Since this is a low poly shape we don't have to be overly detailed; we're just indicating that there is an eye socket here. Grab the middle vertex in the eye socket and [k]G,X[/k] to move it in (Image 20).

image.caption: Image 16 - Inset is a great way to add topology in an area
Image 17 - Move the vertices into an eye shape
Image 18 - Check other perspectives to make sure the eye socket is right
Image 19 - Moving vertices into place
Image 20 - Bringing in the eye socket

content: If you want to give the eye a more dramatic look, move the front vertices down to angle it from the front, and move the bottom vertices up to give it a bit of a squint (Image 21). Predators have their eyes in front for stereo vision, so grab the vertices at the front of the eye and [k]G,X[/k] to move them in (Image 22). Also, move the back ones out, to angle the eye from front to back.

image.caption: Image 21 - Squinting the eye to look more dangerous
Image 22 - Move the eyes forward for predators

content: [k]3[/k] into Face Mode and in the Front perspective view select the inner faces of the mouth (Image 23). [k]I[/k] to inset the faces. We want them to exclude the boundary, so [k]I,B[/k] if you need to (Image 24). We want to extrude these faces, and then sink them into the mouth. First, we will do the extrusion  and set the new faces in place ([k]E,LMB[/k]). Be sure to turn off [k]Auto Merge Vertices[/k] (Image 25) before extruding or the vertices created for the extrusion will get merged with the existing ones. Next, we will sink the faces into the mouth with [k]Alt-S[/k]; this extrudes the faces according to their normals (Image 26). If you bring the faces in too much they will overlap through the jaw; you can [k]G,X[/k] to bring them in and then [k]Alt-S[/k] to shrink.

image.caption: Image 23 - Selecting the inner mouth faces
Image 24 - Insetting the faces
Image 25 - Turn off Auto Merge Vertices when extruding in place
Image 26 - Extruding along the normals

content: In Object Mode, hide the reference images and rotate the dinosaur so it is oriented head-to-tail on the x-axis (Image 1). [k]Shift-A,Mesh,Grid[/k] to add a Grid. Give it 100 subdivisions on the x- and y-axes in order to add topology, and scale it up to 60m (Image 2). Go into the Sculpting workspace, and choose the Grab Brush. If you're not sure which one that is, you can widen the brush dialog with your mouse (Image 3). With the Grab Brush selected, [k]F[/k] to enlarge it (Image 4), and start grabbing topology in the back to make some mountains (Image 5). Make sure to not raise them too high that you are also pulling up the edges. Next, grab the land around the dinosaur to slightly raise it up to create some hills and uneven surface areas (Image 6).

image.caption: Image 1 - Orienting the dinosaur on the x-axis
Image 2 - Adding a grid
Image 3 - Widening the Brush dialog
Image 4 - Enlarging the Grab Brush
Image 5 - Sculpting some mountains
Image 6 - Adding some undulation to the land around the dinosaur

content: Go back into the Layout workspace and with the grid selected, add the [url]Decimate Modifier.^^../Simple Models/The Decimate Modifier[/url]

Take the Ratio down to 0.01, enough so that the Face Count for the goes goes to below 200 and the mountains have a chunky, low poly look (Image 7). Decimate is a destructive modifier, so before applying it, we will want to create a backup. [k]Shift-D[/k] to duplicate the landscape, and [k]M[/k] to move it to a new collection. Then hide the selection and apply the modifier to the original. Then, [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode and you can start moving vertices around if you want (Image 8). You could turn on Proportional Editing and use the mouse wheel to enlarge your circle of influence in order to make the editing more like sculpting.

image.caption: Image 7 - Decimating the landscape
Image 8 - Adjusting the mountain's shape after applying Decimate

content: We'll want to add some foliage to our landscape using trees. These will be just simple pyramids placed around the landscape. In Object Mode, [k]Shift-A,Mesh,Cone[/k] and bring the vertex count to 4 to make it a pyramid (Image 1). Move the object origin to the base of the pyramid, and then [k]S,Z[/k] to make it taller (Image 2).

image.caption: Image 1 - Adding a Cone and making it a pyramid
Image 2 - Making the tree taller than the dinosaur (note the origin is at the base)

content: [k]Numpad7[/k] into Top View. We need to create a forest of trees, so with the first selected, [k]Alt-D[/k] to create a linked duplicate and the [k]R[/k] to rotate it to give some variation (Image 3). Then select both trees and [k]Alt-D[/k] again and [k]R[/k] to Rotate again (Image 4). Make sure the Transform Pivot Point is set to Individual Origins. Keep duplicating, moving, and rotation until you have a nice set of trees (Image 5).

image.caption: Image 3 - Duplicate the original tree and rotate it for variation
Image 4 - Creating a set of trees, using Rotation and Scale to add variation
Image 5 - A forest of trees

content: Go into the Shading workspace and select a tree. Give it a new green colour (Image 6). As long as the trees are linked, all trees should get the same colour. Select the dinosaur and give it a reddish-brown colour (Image 7). Finally, give the mountains a whitish-brown colour (Image 8).

image.caption: Image 6 - Adding a green material to the trees
Image 7 - Reddish-brown for the Dinosaur
Image 8 - Beige for the mountains

key_concepts: The goal of this unit is to use nodes to add a gradient to the mountains.

content: If you don't have your viewport split into two screens, do so now. In the right viewport, change it over to the Shader Editor and make sure the Shader Type is set to Object, not World (Image 1). Select the dinosaur in the left viewport, and you will see its material appear to the right (Image 2).

image.caption: Image 1 - Settingup the viewport
Image 2 - Selecting an object will bring up its shader nodes

content: In the left viewport, in Object Mode, select the landscape. [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode, [k]3[/k] and select all the mountain faces. [k]P,S[/k] to separate the mountains by the selected faces (Image 4). Rename the new object to 'mountains' and give thr ground its own material and color.

image.caption: Image 3 - Selecting the mountain faces
Image 4 - Separating the mountains from the ground

content: We want to turn on the Node Wrangler tool so go to [k]Edit > Preferences > Add-ons[/k] and enable the Node Wrangler add-on. This gives us more options in the Shader Editor.

In the Shader Editor, select the Principled BSDF node and press [k]Ctrl-T[/k]. This is a shortcut that adds a Texture Coordinate Node, Mapping Node, and an Image Texture Node to your shader (Image 5). Delete the Mapping and Image Texture nodes; we will use the Texture Coordinate node to create a gradient going upwards from dark to light. We want to be able to tell Blender that the mountain's shade will be darker the lower its z-value is. [k]Shift-A > Converter > Separate XYZ[/k] and connect the Object output from the Texture Coordinate to the Vector input of the Separate XYZ node (Image 6). Connect the Z output to the Base Color input of the Principled BSDF. You should see the gradient applied across the z-axis (Image 7).

image.caption: Image 5 - The Node Wrangler adds shortcuts to the Shader Editor
Image 6 - Connecting the Separate XYZ node
Image 7 - Connecting all nodes and seeing the gradient

content: Right now the gradient is only black and white, but we want to add a ramp and some colour. [k]Shift-A > Converter > Color Ramp[/k] and put that in between the Separate XYZ and Principled BSDF nodes. Play with the levels in the Color Ramp. If you don't see the expected results, experiment with other outputs from the Texture Coordinate node other than Object.
